reviewBoundary: Eight explicitly authored original complete paired-reading practices. Each group has two full passages with five four-option questions each; frozen originals provide level and task structure only. Same-author entailment, unique-key and all-distractor audit, not independent teacher/learner calibration, official CET provenance, publication or production approval.

units.title: 四级阅读：茅膏菜的营养与雪晶的形态

materials.title: A Green Plant with Sticky Leaves
materials.text:
At a college greenhouse, a display of sundews attracted visitors who wanted to watch a plant catch an insect. Sticky droplets on the leaves held small prey, and the plant could obtain nutrients from it. A visitor concluded that the sundew must no longer need light because it could get all its food from insects.

The greenhouse tutor separated two questions. The plant’s green tissues could use light in photosynthesis, contributing the energy-rich substances needed for growth. Captured prey supplied nutrients that could be scarce in the conditions to which the plant was adapted. Obtaining those nutrients did not replace every function of light.

The tutor did not present insect capture as a sign that the sundew lived like an animal in every respect. The plant combined features of its own way of growing. A familiar label, carnivorous, identified one important behaviour without describing the complete movement of energy and materials through the organism.

The display also warned visitors not to test the leaves by feeding them arbitrary pieces of food. The greenhouse’s care followed its own procedures. A successful capture seen during a short visit was not a complete guide to keeping the species healthy. Soil, water, light and the plant’s condition still mattered.

For the information card, students drew separate arrows for the roles discussed in class. They kept the striking insect story, but connected it with the less visible processes the plant also used. The tutor wanted curiosity to lead to a fuller explanation rather than let one dramatic action stand for the whole organism.

The revised card described what visitors might see without promising a capture at every moment. A sundew resting between events remained the same kind of plant. Its interest did not disappear merely because the most noticeable part of its life was temporarily out of view.

questions.prompt: What mistaken conclusion did one visitor draw?
options: The sticky leaves had a role in catching prey.
Catching insects removed the plant’s need for light.
The plant could obtain nutrients from an insect.
The greenhouse contained green tissues.
questions.explanation: B正确：访客由捕虫推不再需光，老师分能量和营养纠正。A、C是原文确认事实；D温室有绿植物不属被纠正论断。

questions.prompt: What distinction does the tutor make?
options: Visible leaves and invisible insects are unrelated.
A sundew becomes an animal after every capture.
Every nutrient comes only from photosynthesis.
Light-supported production of energy-rich substances differs from nutrients obtained through prey.
questions.explanation: D正确：光合形成富能物与猎物补某营养功能不同。A无无关说；B未变动物；C猎物有营养作用。

questions.prompt: How is the label carnivorous used?
options: To name a behaviour without claiming it describes every process in the plant.
To show that the plant has no green tissues.
To guarantee an insect is caught continuously.
To remove soil and water from the care account.
questions.explanation: A正确：标签指出一重要行为，非全能量物质流程。B仍绿；C捕捉有间歇；D土水等仍重要。

questions.prompt: Why did the information card use separate arrows?
options: To make the plant appear larger than it was.
To replace every explanation with the word animal.
To connect the dramatic capture with other processes and their different roles.
To invite visitors to feed any household food.
questions.explanation: C正确：区分课堂角色并联其他过程，不能一奇观代整体。A无放大目的；B仍解释植物；D明确不随便喂。

questions.prompt: What does the final paragraph imply?
options: A brief absence of the striking event does not erase the organism’s relevant characteristics.
Only continuously active displays have educational value.
A plant without visible capture has stopped belonging to its species.
The revised card promised exactly when prey would arrive.
questions.explanation: A正确：间歇休止仍同类植物仍有趣，短观不包全生命。C、B反原意；D不保证每刻发生。

materials.title: The Pattern That Grew in the Cloud
materials.text:
During a winter lesson, students compared photographs of snow crystals. Some were broad plates, some had branching arms and others looked unlike the familiar star on a holiday card. The teacher asked the class to treat the pictures as different growth histories rather than mistakes in one ideal pattern.

The structure of ice helped explain a common sixfold organisation, but conditions during growth affected the form that developed. Temperature and the water vapour available around a crystal could change as it moved through a cloud. Different parts of its journey could therefore contribute to a complex final shape.

A student asked whether the pictures proved that no two snowflakes could ever be alike. The teacher declined that conclusion. A small collection of photographs could show variety without establishing a universal statement about every crystal that had ever formed. Similarity also depended on which details were being compared and at what scale.

The class examined the photographs’ preparation notes. Some images showed individual crystals selected for their clear shapes. Others showed damaged or partly melted material. A striking published example was not necessarily a representative sample of everything falling during a storm. The selection process had helped create the gallery the students were now admiring.

For their report, students described the patterns they could see and the limits of the collection. They did not use one damaged arm as evidence that ice had lost every regular structural property, nor one perfect-looking star as proof that all snow arrived that way.

The lesson kept wonder while changing the claim behind it. The photographs made variation visible. Understanding the roles of structure, changing conditions and selection made that variation something the class could investigate, rather than a reason to invent one story that every pictured crystal had to follow.

questions.prompt: How does the teacher interpret the varied crystal forms?
options: As evidence that the photographs must all be faulty.
As proof that every falling crystal has a holiday-card shape.
As outcomes of growth histories under changing conditions.
As objects unaffected by the structure of ice.
questions.explanation: C正确：形态是生长结构与云中条件经历，非统一理想型失败。A没说全拍错；B图有多种；D冰结构仍解释六重常见组织。

questions.prompt: What could change during a crystal’s journey?
options: Temperature and available water vapour.
The number of classrooms studying it.
Only the name assigned after the photograph.
The meaning of every ice structure.
questions.explanation: A正确：第二段明确温度水汽随云中历程可变。C不是仅命名；B非生长条件；D未说结构无定含义。

questions.prompt: Why did the teacher avoid the claim that no two snowflakes are alike?
options: The class had found no visible variation.
The collection included every snow crystal ever formed.
The teacher believed every snowflake was identical.
A limited collection and an unspecified scale of comparison could not establish that universal claim.
questions.explanation: D正确：少量图示多样不证全宇宙无同，且相似取决尺度。A有变化；B样本有限；C非转断都同。

questions.prompt: What role did image selection play?
options: It guaranteed every damaged crystal had a different chemical structure.
It could favour clear, striking crystals over a representative view of all falling material.
It made preparation notes unnecessary.
It proved a published picture described the entire storm.
questions.explanation: B正确：精选清晰形不必代表整场雪所有物，须看准备记录。A破损不证化学结构全异；C笔记正重要；D不可全风暴化。

questions.prompt: What is the report encouraged to do?
options: Replace the sixfold organisation with one ideal star pattern.
Discard all imperfect-looking crystals as irrelevant.
Describe observed variation while keeping structural, environmental and sampling limits visible.
Treat a damaged arm as proof that ice has no regular properties.
questions.explanation: C正确：保所见、结构条件取样边界，不以单例全定。A不是统一理想星；B没全弃不完美；D被明确拒。

units.title: 四级阅读：即兴表演的约定与排版的字距

materials.title: Accepting the Scene, Choosing the Action
materials.text:
At a college drama workshop, one student began a scene by saying that the lift had stopped. Her partner replied, “No, we are standing in a garden.” The tutor paused the exercise. The second line had removed the shared situation before the actors could explore it.

The group was practising a principle sometimes called accepting an offer. In this context, an offer was a contribution to the imagined scene. Accepting it meant allowing that established detail to become part of the shared fiction. It did not mean that a character had to agree with every suggestion made by another character.

The partners tried again. This time, the second actor accepted the stopped lift but played someone who refused to press a particular button. The characters could now disagree while the actors cooperated in sustaining the same situation. Conflict inside the story was different from cancelling the story’s premise.

A later exercise introduced a sound outside an imagined window. One actor decided it was rain, and the other connected it with a leaking roof. The scene developed from listening and adding, not from each performer waiting to deliver a separate prepared idea. The tutor still allowed participants to stop the activity under the workshop’s agreed boundaries. A theatrical principle was not permission to ignore a real person’s limits.

For feedback, the group identified the moment when an action either supported or erased a shared detail. They did not rank performers by how often their characters said yes. A character could refuse, hesitate or argue and still contribute to a coherent scene.

The students left with a more precise task than always agree. They were learning to distinguish the imagined facts they built together from the choices a character could make within them. That distinction gave them more possibilities for action, rather than forcing every scene towards a polite conversation in which nothing could happen.

questions.prompt: Why did the tutor stop the first exchange?
options: The actors had spoken too softly for any listener.
The first actor had forgotten a fixed script.
The lift had physically broken in the workshop.
The second actor contradicted the established setting instead of building within it.
questions.explanation: D正确：后句抹掉已建立停梯情境，未让共同场景发展。A没音量问题；C是虚构情境；B即兴非固定本。

questions.prompt: What does accepting an offer mean in this exercise?
options: Making every character approve every proposed action.
Keeping a contribution to the imagined situation available for development.
Removing all conflict from the story.
Agreeing to any real-world request outside the workshop.
questions.explanation: B正确：接纳共同虚构事实，不等角色全赞同行动或真人无限同意。A、C误合人物与演员合作；D现实边界仍在。

questions.prompt: Why could refusal to press a button work in the second attempt?
options: It established that the actors were actually in a garden.
It erased the stopped lift from the scene.
The character disagreed while the actors retained the same fictional premise.
It replaced cooperation with unrelated speeches.
questions.explanation: C正确：承认停梯仍可角色拒按钮，演员合作与剧情冲突可并存。A、B不是新场景；D仍互接。

questions.prompt: What did the rain and leaking-roof exchange demonstrate?
options: Responding to another contribution can develop a shared scene.
Each actor should ignore unexpected information.
The best scene requires no listening.
A new detail always cancels what preceded it.
questions.explanation: A正确：听并加雨及漏屋顶关联，让戏共同发展。B、C相反；D新增可延伸非必抹前。

questions.prompt: How was feedback focused?
options: On the literal number of yes answers.
On whether actions preserved or erased a shared detail.
On proving all characters should be polite.
On forcing participants beyond their agreed limits.
questions.explanation: B正确：找具体支持或取消共同细节的时刻，不按字面yes次数，现实限度保。A、C、D均非规则。

materials.title: The Space Between the Letters
materials.text:
A student magazine enlarged the title of an article and expected the heading to become easier to read. The letters were large, but some readers still hesitated over the word. The designer found that the space between two particular letters made them appear joined, while another gap seemed to divide the word in the middle.

The team first increased every gap by the same amount. This improved one pair but made another too loose. The visual shapes of letters differed, so equal measured distances did not necessarily produce equal-looking spaces. The designer adjusted individual pairs and compared the result at the size intended for publication.

A reduced preview was useful for the whole page but could hide the problem in a large heading. Conversely, judging only the enlarged title left out its relationship with the surrounding text. The team inspected both levels. The question was not whether one image size was always correct, but what each view allowed them to examine.

They also kept the wording fixed during the comparison. A rewritten title might be easier because its letters or language changed, making it harder to identify the contribution of spacing. The final choice considered the intended heading and layout, not a claim that the same numerical setting would suit every typeface.

Readers’ comments helped locate uncertainty, but the magazine did not describe the short check as a complete study of all readers. It used a practical result for a defined page. The designer recorded the adjusted pairs so a later revision would not silently return to the original problem.

The finished heading looked simple. That simplicity had come from attending to the relationships among shapes, scale and context. Making letters bigger was one operation; making the particular word readable in its final place required more specific judgement.

questions.prompt: Why did enlargement alone not solve the heading problem?
options: Some gaps made letters seem joined or divided the word visually.
Every reader had received a different word.
The letters had all been removed.
The magazine printed only spoken recordings.
questions.explanation: A正确：字大仍有特定间隔造成黏合或中裂，大小非唯一因素。C字在；B比较保持同词；D是印排。

questions.prompt: What did increasing all gaps equally show?
options: Equal distances always create equal-looking visual spacing.
The heading required no individual adjustment.
Typeface shape had no effect on appearance.
A uniform numerical change could help one pair but make another worse.
questions.explanation: D正确：同增距一对好另一松，字形差需个别调。A、B、C与实际试验相反。

questions.prompt: Why inspect both reduced and enlarged views?
options: Only one view contained the actual wording.
They reveal different aspects of the heading and its page context.
They guarantee identical reactions from all readers.
A small preview can measure every large-letter detail accurately.
questions.explanation: B正确：缩图看整页可能藏大标题问题，放大又漏周文关系，须双层。A词未换；C非全读者保证；D小预览不见尽细节。

questions.prompt: Why was the wording kept fixed?
options: To stop readers understanding the article.
To prove all titles need the same setting.
To avoid confusing a spacing effect with a change in the title’s letters or language.
To replace the layout with a list of numbers.
questions.explanation: C正确：改词也会影响易读，固定才较清楚看字距贡献。A非阻读；B不泛化字体；D仍版面评判。

questions.prompt: What claim did the magazine make about the check?
options: It supported a practical decision for a defined page, with limited generalisation.
It established one permanent numerical rule for typography.
It measured every reader’s behaviour in all typefaces.
It showed size should never be changed.
questions.explanation: A正确：短检查限具体页，记调整免回旧错，不是全部阅读研究。C、B过广；D只是放大不总够，非永不改大。

units.title: 四级阅读：行李标签的终点与座位预订的路段

materials.title: The Other Airport in the Same City
materials.text:
For a fictional travel workshop, Mei was given an itinerary showing a flight to a city with two airports. The shortened booking summary displayed only the city name. Mei first chose the airport she recognised from a previous visit and planned a meeting there.

The full itinerary named the other airport and gave its code. A tutor asked Mei to compare the current document with the older journey rather than use familiarity as confirmation. The city could be the same while the arrival location differed. A code was useful when it was connected to the named airport, not merely copied as an unexplained string of letters.

The workshop then supplied a sample baggage tag for the current journey. It listed a connecting airport as well as the final destination. Mei checked the field explicitly marked as the destination, rather than assume the first airport code she noticed identified where the bag would be collected. The connection showed part of the route, not a separate instruction to end the journey there.

An old label remained on the practice suitcase. The group discussed why staff had to distinguish the current tag from a previous one. A familiar name on the bag could be historical information. It did not override the active record for the new journey.

The exercise did not claim that every real airline used one identical layout. It asked participants to read the labels and fields in the document before them and ask the responsible service when the meaning was unclear. Mei changed the planned meeting place after checking the complete airport information.

Her final checklist was short: confirm the particular location, the role of the field and the relevant journey. It was more useful than memorising one city-to-airport association. The goal was to connect a travel record with the event it actually described, especially where a shortened display hid a distinction that mattered.

questions.prompt: Why was the city name insufficient for Mei’s first plan?
options: The itinerary showed no arrival city at all.
The city had changed its name during the flight.
The city had two airports and the shortened summary did not identify which one.
Every airport in the workshop had the same code.
questions.explanation: C正确：同城双机场，摘要只列城名，熟悉机场未必本次。B无改名；A有城市；D代码区分具体机场。

questions.prompt: What did the full itinerary establish?
options: The particular airport and code for this arrival.
The airport Mei had used on every earlier trip.
A guarantee that the baggage tag had no connecting field.
The meeting partner’s private address.
questions.explanation: A正确：完整行程明确另一个机场及代码，遂改会合地。B不是全部旧旅；C标签有转机；D没私址。

questions.prompt: Why did Mei check the marked destination field on the baggage tag?
options: Every printed code had an identical role.
The connection was always the place to collect all bags.
The old label was the only current record.
The first noticed code could refer to a connection rather than the final destination.
questions.explanation: D正确：标签有中转及终点，不能首见一码即认终点。A角色不同；B转机非本练习终止指令；C旧标历史不覆盖当前。

questions.prompt: What does the old suitcase label illustrate?
options: A previous journey automatically determines the next route.
Information attached to an object can belong to an earlier event.
The newest itinerary should be ignored when a name is familiar.
A bag cannot carry historical information.
questions.explanation: B正确：旧名可能旧行程，须分当前记录。A、C都反现用记录；D正可有历史标。

questions.prompt: What is the exercise’s broader recommendation?
options: Choose the first code visible in every document.
Treat all airlines’ layouts as identical.
Identify the location, field role and current journey rather than rely only on a familiar place name.
Avoid asking for clarification of a field.
questions.explanation: C正确：末段三项，并承认真实版式可异应问负责服务。B不一概；A、D反读字段和澄清要求。

materials.title: The Empty Seat Before Middleton
materials.text:
On a fictional intercity train, Rafael found an empty seat with a display reading reserved from Middleton. He was travelling beyond Middleton and assumed empty meant available for the rest of his journey. A staff member explained the service’s stated rule: the seat could be used before that station, but a later reservation applied from there.

The display described a segment, not the entire route. Current occupancy and future allocation were different questions. Rafael could observe that nobody was sitting there without knowing whether someone would board later. The empty seat was real; the conclusion about its availability for the whole journey was not supported.

The staff member helped him find a place matching the relevant part of his trip. They checked the service and date as well as the destination, since several trains made similar journeys. A reservation for another departure would not establish a claim on this one merely because the route name looked familiar.

Rafael also learned that a changed seating plan could require staff to direct passengers under the service’s procedure. The workshop’s account did not tell readers to settle every disagreement by taking the display as an unlimited authority. It showed what this particular message meant within the stated arrangement and where to seek a current decision.

Later, Rafael described the mistake as reading a present observation as a future promise. The station name on the display had been important information rather than decoration. Once he connected it to the time and section for which a place was allocated, the message became useful.

An empty object, a valid ticket and a reservation were related parts of the journey, but they were not interchangeable evidence. The lesson was to ask which portion of the trip a statement covered before assuming it applied from departure to arrival.

questions.prompt: What did reserved from Middleton mean under the stated rule?
options: The seat had to remain empty for the entire day.
A reservation began at a later station, although it could be used earlier.
No one could ever sit there after Middleton.
Rafael’s ticket was invalid on every part of the train.
questions.explanation: B正确：本服务可在Middleton前用，之后有预订，非全天状态。A、C非规则；D未说车票全无效。

questions.prompt: What could Rafael’s observation of emptiness directly establish?
options: That no future passenger had a claim.
That he had selected the correct date.
That nobody occupied the seat at that moment.
That every display in the carriage was wrong.
questions.explanation: C正确：现没人不证将来分配，空事实与全程可用推论分。A超时段；B没由空位证日期；D无全屏错误。

questions.prompt: Why check the service and date?
options: Similar routes could belong to different departures and reservation records.
Any similar route name created the same reservation.
The display contained no station name.
Every train used a unique destination name.
questions.explanation: A正确：同样旅程多班，另一出发的预订不自动对应本班。D非唯一地名；B正反；C有Middleton。

questions.prompt: What does the paragraph about changed seating plans add?
options: A seat display is always an unlimited legal authority.
Passengers should decide every conflict without staff.
A changed plan proves all reservations meaningless.
The meaning of a display operates within a current service procedure, with staff available to handle changes.
questions.explanation: D正确：有调整依程序由员工指引，消息作用非无限，需找当前决定。B不应自断全冲突；C未全否；A明确非无限权威。

questions.prompt: What inference error is central to the story?
options: Mistaking a future reservation for a past journey.
Extending a present observation or segment-specific statement to the whole future trip.
Assuming a valid ticket always contains no destination.
Treating every station name as a passenger’s name.
questions.explanation: B正确：把现在空与某段说明扩大成全程可用，末段点明时段范围。A不是主误；C、D不是文本事件。

units.title: 四级阅读：节拍中的快慢与画作复制品的裁切

materials.title: More Notes Between the Beats
materials.text:
At a percussion workshop, a student said the second passage must be faster because it contained more strikes. The tutor asked the class to keep tapping the underlying beat while listening to the described pattern. The beat remained at the same rate, but the player divided the spaces between beats into more events.

The distinction was between tempo and the number of notes within that tempo. A busier surface could feel more energetic without the basic pulse speeding up. The tutor used a steady reference and asked students to identify which change they meant before describing the passage as faster.

Loudness introduced another confusion. Stronger strikes attracted attention and made one group seem more forceful. They did not automatically shorten the time between beats. A performer could change level and rate together, but the class needed to recognise them as separate choices before discussing a particular example.

For practice, one group maintained the pulse while another played a more divided pattern. The task made the relationship visible through coordination, not through counting every sound as a new beat. When the groups lost contact, they stopped and returned to the common reference rather than simply play louder.

The tutor did not demand that all music have one obvious pulse. The exercise concerned the pattern the class had been given. It helped them distinguish rate, subdivision and level in a case where those features could be examined separately.

In their notes, students replaced a vague claim that the second passage was faster with a more specific description. It had more events between equal beats and a stronger level in one section. Naming the changes made comparison easier while leaving the question of their musical effect open for discussion.

questions.prompt: Why did the second passage seem faster to the student?
options: More strikes occurred within the same beat spacing.
The reference had been removed from the room.
Its underlying beat had disappeared.
The tutor had changed every instrument’s size.
questions.explanation: A正确：表面更多击点但基本拍速未变，音符细分增。C拍在；B有稳参照；D没改尺寸。

questions.prompt: What did the steady reference help identify?
options: Whether every musical piece has the same rhythm.
The age of the percussion instrument.
Whether the underlying pulse changed rather than only its subdivisions.
The correct volume for all future performances.
questions.explanation: C正确：参照让分拍速和拍内事件量，不是全音乐统一规范。A、D过广；B无年龄测量。

questions.prompt: What did stronger strikes establish on their own?
options: A guaranteed increase in tempo.
A change in level, not necessarily a shorter interval between beats.
A new beat for every audible event.
A loss of all structure in the pattern.
questions.explanation: B正确：力度音量可强而拍距未必短；速率和级别分。A非保证；C细分不全是新拍；D未失结构。

questions.prompt: Why did the two groups coordinate around a pulse?
options: To avoid hearing one another.
To prove that louder playing always restores timing.
To remove every note from the passage.
To explore the relation between a common beat and a more divided pattern.
questions.explanation: D正确：一组维脉冲一组细分，关系靠协调，失去联系回参照非加响。A相反；C仍有音；B明确不只大声。

questions.prompt: How did the final notes improve the description?
options: They named changes in subdivision and level instead of using one ambiguous label.
They selected the one correct emotional response.
They declared every energetic passage faster.
They assumed every kind of music had an identical pulse.
questions.explanation: A正确：改说等拍内事件多及某段更强，分清变化而效果仍可议。C、D泛化；B未定唯一感受。

materials.title: The Figure at the Edge of the Postcard
materials.text:
A museum shop sold a postcard of a landscape painting. The card showed a bright house beside a lake, but a visitor noticed that the original also contained a small figure at the far left. The reproduction had been cropped to fit the card’s shape, leaving that part outside the printed image.

The crop made the house appear more dominant. It did not physically alter the painting, and the card could still be useful as a detail. The problem arose when the shop described it as the full painting without qualification. A reader could then form an interpretation from a selection while believing the selection was the whole work.

The curator compared several reproductions. One showed the complete composition at a smaller scale; another enlarged the figure but left out much of the lake. Each supported a different kind of inspection. The enlarged detail made clothing easier to see, while the complete view showed how the figure related to the space around it.

For the revised display, the shop labelled the cropped card as a detail and provided a complete small image nearby. It also checked that the printed colours were described appropriately rather than guaranteed identical under every viewing condition. The revised information did not make the detail worthless. It gave visitors a route between the selection and the composition from which it came.

The visitor’s discovery became part of a short museum activity. Participants described how the apparent balance changed across views. They were not asked to guess the painter’s private intentions from the missing figure alone. They could examine an observable effect of cropping while keeping a historical claim about intention separate.

A small reproduction could invite interest in a large work. Its value increased when the frame around the reproduction was understood as an editorial choice, not mistaken for the boundary of the original painting.

questions.prompt: Why was the figure absent from the postcard?
options: The painter had erased it from the original.
The postcard was made before the figure existed in any version.
The visitor had examined a different museum.
The reproduction cropped away part of the composition.
questions.explanation: D正确：为卡形裁去左边，原画仍有人。A原画未删；C同画；B无创作版本先后证据。

questions.prompt: What was misleading about the shop’s description?
options: It called the cropped view a detail.
It presented the selection as the full painting without qualification.
It offered a small reproduction for sale.
It showed the house beside a lake.
questions.explanation: B正确：裁图可有用，但无说明称全画使读者误以全构图。A后来正改detail；C售小图不自动误导；D景物实有。

questions.prompt: What did the complete small view offer that the enlarged figure detail did not?
options: A guarantee of exact colour under every lamp.
A physical replacement for the original canvas.
The figure’s relationship with the surrounding composition.
The painter’s undisclosed intentions.
questions.explanation: C正确：全景示人与周空间关系，放大细节看衣却漏湖。A未保所有照明色同；B不替实物；D图不证私意。

questions.prompt: How did the revised display treat the cropped card?
options: It identified the selection and linked it with a complete view.
It removed every reproduction as worthless.
It announced that cropping never changes visual balance.
It hid the original painting from visitors.
questions.explanation: A正确：标detail旁给全小图，提供部分到整体路径。B未全弃；C活动看平衡变；D没藏原画。

questions.prompt: What distinction did the activity preserve?
options: A detail and a complete view must always have identical effects.
The visitor had to decide one final meaning for all viewers.
A postcard’s edge is necessarily the original painting’s edge.
An observed effect of cropping does not alone establish the artist’s private intention.
questions.explanation: D正确：观察裁切平衡变化与推作者私意分，不由缺人猜定。A效果可异；C卡边是编辑选择；B无唯一全观者意义任务。

units.title: 六级阅读：指示手势的共同语境与冰川末端的位置

materials.title: The Place Meant by Here
materials.text:
In a fictional planning meeting, a speaker pointed at a map and said that the entrance should move here. Everyone could see the gesture, but later notes identified two different locations. The finger’s direction had crossed several marks. Seeing the movement was not the same as establishing which feature the speaker intended the group to consider.

Pointing can be efficient because people use shared surroundings and expectations to interpret it. Its success does not require the direction alone to encode a unique coordinate. Listeners consider what has been discussed, what the speaker is attending to and which proposal would make sense at that moment. The resulting interpretation can be reasonable and still require correction if another listener has selected a different referent.

The group repaired the misunderstanding through a question. One participant named the corner she thought was meant; the speaker clarified that he intended the neighbouring gate. This exchange did more than add extra words to a message already complete. It helped establish the common reference on which the next decision depended. The correction showed that common understanding could be achieved without having been identical from the start.

A later remote meeting introduced another difficulty. Participants had opened different versions of the map, and a shared-screen pointer did not identify the same visible feature in every local copy. The team named the version and the relevant location before continuing. The technology transmitted an action, but the interpretation depended on which representation a person had in front of them.

For its record, the group distinguished the observed gesture from the confirmed referent. A note saying that the speaker pointed was not itself a complete statement of where the entrance had been proposed. The final minutes included the named feature and the decision. They did not treat every inference from a video frame as a direct statement of intention.

When notes later went to an absent colleague, the bare word here was particularly unhelpful. The record needed a description that could travel without the original gesture and shared table.

The lesson was not that gestures were unreliable or that every conversation needed a fully specified description before anyone spoke. Shared context made ordinary communication workable. The important practice was to recognise when it had not yet secured the intended reference. A short clarification could preserve the efficiency of pointing while preventing an apparently shared detail from quietly dividing the reasoning of the group.

questions.prompt: What caused the disagreement in the opening example?
options: No participant could see the map or the speaker.
The gesture was visible but did not by itself select one intended map feature for every listener.
The speaker had explicitly named both locations as identical.
The meeting had made no use of shared surroundings.
questions.explanation: B正确：指向穿过多标，见手势不等同认定意指对象。A都可见；C未明确同一；D靠地图共享情境但解读可异。

questions.prompt: What role does shared context play?
options: It makes a finger encode an exact coordinate independently of the audience.
It replaces the need to identify a referent after a disagreement appears.
It requires every listener to have identical knowledge before the first word.
It helps listeners interpret an efficient gesture, while still leaving room for correction.
questions.explanation: D正确：语境期待辅助推意可高效，但合理解释仍可需修。A不是几何独立编码；C可通过对话达共同；B分歧后需确指。

questions.prompt: What did the clarification exchange accomplish?
options: It proved the first gesture had been physically invisible.
It showed the map contained only one gate.
It established a common reference that had not been fully shared initially.
It removed all need for further planning decisions.
questions.explanation: C正确：命名角点后改邻门，修复共同对象再决策。A非不可见；B无唯一路门；D仍继续决策。

questions.prompt: Why did the remote meeting need a version check?
options: The transmitted action could be interpreted against different representations.
A local file always contains the same features as any shared screen.
Map versions determine the speaker’s private intention without conversation.
Every digital pointer automatically changes the underlying plan.
questions.explanation: A正确：各开不同版，指针传到动作不保证同可见特征，须名版本位置。D不自动改图；B正不同；C版本本身不读私意。

questions.prompt: What is the concluding recommendation?
options: Record a gesture as proof of whatever location a viewer infers.
Replace all gestures with exhaustive descriptions in every exchange.
Use shared context efficiently but clarify when it has not secured the intended referent.
Assume a reasonable initial interpretation cannot later need correction.
questions.explanation: C正确：非弃手势或全规格长话，认未共指时短问。B过度；A把推断作意图事实；D合理初解也可修。

materials.title: The Front of the Glacier
materials.text:
A line marking the front of a glacier is visually powerful. Two dated photographs can show that the ice edge has moved, making the boundary an appealing summary of change. A fictional geography class used such images to ask what the front could establish about a glacier and which further questions required other evidence.

The front reflected processes including the movement of ice towards it and losses near the edge. Its position could change when their relationship changed. An advance did not automatically show that the entire glacier had gained mass; a flow change could redistribute ice. Nor was the distance of retreat by itself a complete measure of the amount lost from a glacier of varying width and thickness.

The students therefore distinguished position, area, volume and mass balance. Estimating one from another required assumptions and measurements, not merely a more precise line on the photograph. A narrow section and a broad section could contribute differently to a distance-based comparison. The class kept the geometry visible in its reasoning rather than treat every metre of front movement as an identical quantity of ice.

Time and image conditions mattered too. Seasonal snow could obscure a boundary, and photographs taken at different points in a seasonal cycle might invite an incomplete comparison. The group recorded dates, viewpoints and the features used to identify ice rather than snow. It did not discard the photographs; it described the observations they supported and where interpretation entered.

A whole-glacier account considered additions and losses over a stated period. The front was one useful indicator within that wider account. To investigate causes, the students also needed evidence about relevant conditions and processes. A local position record could contribute to climate research without becoming, by itself, a complete account of global change or a forecast for every other glacier.

Changes could also occur in thickness away from the front. A stable-looking edge did not certify that every part of the glacier had remained unchanged in the interval.

The final display showed the boundary images beside explanations of geometry, timing and mass. It made the visible change easier to understand without asking one dramatic line to carry every possible conclusion. The students had learned neither that photographs were sufficient for everything nor that an incomplete indicator was worthless. They had learned to connect the question to the quantity the evidence could actually describe, and to name the measurements needed for the next step.

questions.prompt: What does the class question about a glacier front?
options: Which wider quantities and explanations its movement can establish on its own.
Whether a visible boundary can ever be photographed.
Whether every glacier has an identical width.
Which photograph should replace all measurements permanently.
questions.explanation: A正确：以图问末端位移能支持何种冰川变化、何题需其他证。B图可拍；C不假定同宽；D不是选图全代测。

questions.prompt: Why does an advance not automatically prove whole-glacier mass gain?
options: The front has no relationship to ice movement.
Every advance is a camera error.
Changed ice flow can redistribute material towards the edge.
Mass is identical to the number of visible lines.
questions.explanation: C正确：流向前补给与边缘损失关系变，流速可重分配冰，并非全体增质量。A有关系；B非全误；D不等线数。

questions.prompt: Why consider width and thickness when comparing retreat distances?
options: They make dates irrelevant.
They guarantee a photograph contains every hidden feature.
They turn mass balance into a single camera setting.
Equal distances need not correspond to equal volumes of ice.
questions.explanation: D正确：截面几何异同退距失冰体积可异，需要其他测量。A仍要时间；B未保全看见；C质量平衡非拍摄设置。

questions.prompt: What did seasonal snow require the students to do?
options: Treat every white area as permanent glacier ice.
Record image timing and the evidence used to distinguish snow from the relevant ice boundary.
Assume all photographs came from the same seasonal moment.
Remove every photograph from the study.
questions.explanation: B正确：季雪可遮界，核日期视点识别特征，不弃图但限解释。A、C忽略条件；D过否。

questions.prompt: How is the front record finally characterised?
options: A useful indicator whose contribution depends on the quantity and question being examined.
A complete global climate explanation requiring no other evidence.
A meaningless line because it cannot describe every glacier property.
A direct forecast for all other glaciers.
questions.explanation: A正确：可指示但位置面积体积质量及成因问题需各证，不能全包。B、D外推过度；C不是不完整即无用。

units.title: 六级阅读：判例推理的必要理由与食物转运的核算

materials.title: The Sentence Quoted from the Earlier Case
materials.text:
In a fictional legal-reasoning seminar, students examined a system in which certain decisions of a higher court constrained later courts. One student found a broad sentence in an earlier judgement and treated it as the rule deciding a new dispute. The tutor asked why that sentence had mattered to the earlier outcome and how the facts compared.

The exercise distinguished a necessary basis of decision from additional observations. A judgement could discuss an imagined situation to illustrate a concern without deciding that situation. Under the seminar’s stated framework, not every sentence carried the same authority merely because it appeared in the same published document. The relevant question was how the reasoning supported the result and which issue the court had actually resolved.

Facts mattered to that inquiry. Two disputes could share words such as permit or public access while differ in the authority involved and the action challenged. A later court might distinguish a case by explaining a material difference. That was not necessarily ignoring precedent. It was an argument about the scope of what the earlier decision required.

Multiple opinions added another complication. Judges could agree on the result while give different reasons. Counting votes for the outcome did not automatically establish majority support for every passage in one opinion. The students traced the reasoning adopted rather than combine selected sentences from several judges into an argument none had jointly made.

The source also needed to be read as a whole. A quotation in a digest could help locate a case, but its surrounding discussion might qualify a phrase. The tutor kept citation, extract and reasoning separate. Finding the same wording was a beginning for analysis, not a substitute for it.

Later treatment of the earlier case was relevant too. A frequently quoted sentence could have been qualified or distinguished in subsequent decisions. The students checked that history under the exercise’s hierarchy rather than treating popularity in quotations as an independent measure of legal force. The record preserved the route to those later reasons.

The class did not conclude that precedent was infinitely flexible or that a later reader could choose any preferred meaning. Its framework imposed obligations to explain the relevant authority, reasoning and facts. The discipline lay in making that connection examinable. A defensible argument showed why an earlier decision governed, differed or left a question open, rather than let the prestige of a quoted sentence do work its role in the original case did not support.

questions.prompt: Why did the tutor question the broad quotation?
options: All earlier court documents were excluded from the seminar.
A published judgement could contain no reasoning relevant to later cases.
A sentence became binding only if it used the word permit.
Its authority depended on its role in the earlier decision, not only on its presence in the document.
questions.explanation: D正确：须看该句与先案结果的必要关系和事实范围，非同文每句同权。B非全无关；C非关键词机制；A正用旧判。

questions.prompt: What is the function of distinguishing necessary reasoning from additional observations?
options: To erase every illustrative passage from the historical source.
To identify which part carried the relevant decision-making authority under the given framework.
To show that hypothetical examples always decide future disputes.
To make every sentence equally controlling once printed.
questions.explanation: B正确：必要判决基础与旁述权威分，假设例未必已判。A未删史源；C、D正反限定。

questions.prompt: How can factual differences be relevant without simply ignoring precedent?
options: A later argument can identify a material difference limiting the earlier decision’s scope.
Cases are comparable only when every detail is identical.
Any different word removes all obligation to explain.
Shared headings determine the result without further analysis.
questions.explanation: A正确：差异须论何以重要来界定适用，非完全不顾。C无须解释不合；B不要求每细同；D标题非决断。

questions.prompt: Why are votes for an outcome insufficient to assign support to every reason?
options: All judges necessarily wrote the same opinion.
A result can never have more than one rationale.
Judges may agree on the result while disagree on reasoning.
Students had no access to any opinions.
questions.explanation: C正确：同结果可异理，不能把一人每段当多数或拼无人共同论证。A、B与原文相反；D有文本追踪。

questions.prompt: What practice does the ending favour?
options: Treat every digest extract as a complete substitute for the judgement.
Explain the connection among authority, reasons and material facts rather than rely on a prestigious extract alone.
Choose any reading because precedent has no constraints.
Assign equal scope to every example in an opinion.
questions.explanation: B正确：结尾要求可检视适用区别或留空的理由，引用只是分析开头。A、C、D皆抹语境权责。

materials.title: The Food on the Shared Truck
materials.text:
A fictional food-redistribution network collected surplus items from several shops and delivered them to community kitchens. Its monthly report counted kilograms received and kilograms delivered. These were useful operational figures, but the environmental team resisted using one of them as a complete measure of climate benefit.

Food differed in the resources associated with its production and handling. The same mass did not necessarily represent the same emissions. The collection also required transport, packaging and sometimes refrigeration. Listing those activities did not prove that redistribution was environmentally harmful. It identified parts of an account needed before a more specific claim could be made.

Shared routes created an allocation question. A vehicle might visit several donors and carry food for several destinations. Assigning all of the route’s emissions to each donation would count the same activity repeatedly. Assigning none because the truck had travelled anyway could also conceal an additional stop or a changed schedule. The team documented how it divided shared activity and what question that division was intended to answer.

For some decisions, the relevant comparison concerned whether an extra collection would add distance to an existing route. For a report on the network’s total operation, the whole route still belonged in the account. A marginal decision and an organisational total could therefore use related data without being identical measures. The report made the boundary visible instead of select whichever one produced the most attractive result.

The team also asked what would otherwise happen to the food. A product headed for disposal differed from one that would probably have been sold or redistributed through another route. Those alternatives were uncertain and had to be stated as assumptions where evidence was incomplete.

The network also distinguished received material from the portion kitchens could actually use. Sorting losses were recorded rather than counted as meals delivered. This gave an intensity measure a named denominator: emissions per kilogram received and per kilogram usefully delivered were related but different ratios. Neither should be presented without the stage it measured.

Kitchens valued regular access to useful ingredients as well as environmental outcomes. The network reported that service separately rather than convert every nutritional benefit into an invented quantity of saved emissions. The final account described delivered food, operating resources and scenario-based estimates. A meaningful environmental claim could support the work without pretending that kilograms alone settled the question or that one allocation rule answered every possible decision.

questions.prompt: Why were kilograms alone insufficient for the environmental claim?
options: No operational figure could be useful for any purpose.
Every food item had identical handling requirements.
Food production impacts and collection activities could differ despite equal mass.
The network had stopped moving food.
questions.explanation: C正确：同重食品资源排放可异，转运包装冷藏也入账，公斤是运营量非完整气候效果。A过否有用数；B不一样；D仍配送。

questions.prompt: What problem would assigning the full shared-route emissions to every donation create?
options: It could count the same activity multiple times.
It would remove all transport from the report.
It would identify which donor spoke first.
It would prove refrigeration had no effect.
questions.explanation: A正确：一车多捐多目的，给每批全程排放会重记。C不相关；B非去掉；D不证明冷藏无效。

questions.prompt: Why distinguish an extra-stop decision from the organisation’s total?
options: Only a marginal decision can use transport data.
Additional distance and total operation answer different accounting questions.
Both questions necessarily require assigning zero emissions.
The network’s whole route has no environmental meaning.
questions.explanation: B正确：加一停看新增距离，总报仍看全程，边界相关非同数。A总报也用；D全程有义；C不一概零。

questions.prompt: What role do alternatives for the food play?
options: They eliminate the need to examine operating activities.
They can be assumed identical for every item.
They guarantee that every collected product would otherwise be discarded.
They shape the comparison, with uncertain assumptions stated where evidence is incomplete.
questions.explanation: D正确：不收则丢、售或别线再分不同，须说假设；不是全都废弃。B、C过强；A运输仍重要。

questions.prompt: How are the kitchens’ ingredient benefits treated?
options: They are ignored because they are not carbon measures.
They prove the network’s allocation rule is uniquely correct.
They are reported as service benefits without inventing an automatic emissions equivalent.
They make every kilogram an identical climate benefit.
questions.explanation: C正确：营养供应价值另报，不凭空换减排量，仍支持服务。A未忽视；B分配规则依问题；D同重不同影响。

units.title: 六级阅读：劳动生产率的边界与分配公平的标准

materials.title: Output per Worker, Output per Hour
materials.text:
A fictional workshop reported more output per employee after reorganising its production. The headline suggested that each person had become more productive. The evaluator asked which quantity had been divided by which. Output per employee and output per hour could move differently if working hours changed. A ratio needed a named numerator, denominator and period before it could support a particular interpretation.

Measuring output was not entirely straightforward either. Revenue could rise because prices changed, because the product mix changed or because more physical goods were supplied. A money total did not automatically measure an equivalent increase in production volume. Where quality differed, counting objects alone could also miss something relevant. The evaluator described the output measure and its limits rather than assume that one familiar total represented every aspect of what the workshop produced.

The organisational boundary mattered. Some tasks had moved to an outside supplier. If the workshop counted the same final output while removing those workers’ hours from its own denominator, its internal ratio could rise without the full chain requiring less labour. This did not mean outsourcing could never improve efficiency. It meant the firm-level figure and a whole-process comparison answered different questions.

Capital and working conditions also shaped the result. Better equipment or a changed task could alter output without identifying an individual’s effort as the sole cause. A low ratio was therefore not automatically evidence of laziness, just as a high ratio did not by itself establish a worker’s preferred conditions. The report separated description of the measured result from an explanation of why it had occurred.

The figures could still help planning. The workshop compared periods under stated definitions and investigated the effects of its changes. It did not treat a carefully limited measure as useless merely because it lacked every possible dimension. The crucial step was to preserve the boundary and purpose so a later reader could understand what had improved.

A busy period producing unfinished work did not necessarily match the period in which completed output was recorded, so timing also mattered.

Questions about wages, workload and the distribution of gains remained related but distinct. A productivity number alone could not decide them. The final account made the ratio useful by resisting the temptation to turn it into a complete judgement about people, technology and welfare. It described a particular relationship between output and labour under defined conditions, leaving further claims to the evidence they required.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish output per employee from output per hour?
options: They can differ when hours per employee change.
Only one of them can ever be expressed as a ratio.
Employee counts automatically include all outside suppliers.
Neither needs a time period to be interpreted.
questions.explanation: A正确：工时变时每人和每小时可不同，分子分母期间须明。B都可比率；C外包边界恰需查；D要期间。

questions.prompt: Why is a revenue increase not automatically a volume increase?
options: Revenue never contains information about production.
Every product has identical quality.
Prices and product mix can change as well as physical quantity.
The evaluator had defined every good as free.
questions.explanation: C正确：收入受价格组合数量影响，计件也可能漏质量。A非全无信息；B质量可能异；D未零价定义。

questions.prompt: How can outsourcing alter the internal productivity ratio without a whole-process labour saving?
options: It must remove the workshop’s final output entirely.
It guarantees every supplier uses no labour.
It makes organisational boundaries irrelevant.
Some hours can leave the workshop’s denominator while final output remains counted.
questions.explanation: D正确：同最终产出、外移劳动不入本厂工时可推高内部比率，链总工未必减。A、B非必要；C边界关键。

questions.prompt: What inference about workers does the report reject?
options: Recognising that equipment can influence output.
Treating the ratio alone as proof of personal effort or preferred working conditions.
Using a stated measure for a limited planning question.
Comparing periods while retaining definitions.
questions.explanation: B正确：低率不自证懒、高率不自证理想工作条件，设备任务也影响。A、C、D都是文中接受的做法非被拒推论。

questions.prompt: What gives the number practical value?
options: Keeping its definitions and purpose visible while investigating further explanations separately.
Allowing it to decide all wage and welfare questions automatically.
Hiding the outsourcing boundary to simplify the headline.
Assuming physical quantity and revenue always mean the same output.
questions.explanation: A正确：有界度量仍有用，保口径目的，其他因果和分配另证。B越权；C隐边界误导；D混不同量。

materials.title: Half According to Whose Measure?
materials.text:
In a fictional fair-division exercise, two people valued different parts of a divisible cake differently. Equal weight would not necessarily give them equal satisfaction. The tutor therefore described a rule in terms of each person’s own valuation rather than assume a single common scale of taste. For this model, values of separate parts could be added to give the whole’s value.

Under the exercise’s assumptions, one person cut the cake into two parts that they regarded as equally valuable. The other chose the part they preferred. The cutter could not prefer the chosen part to the remaining one because, by the stated construction, they had judged them equal. The chooser had selected the part they preferred. In that two-person model, neither regarded the other’s allocation as better than their own.

The guarantee depended on the procedure and assumptions. It did not mean the pieces had equal mass or market price, that both people had identical tastes, or that a real cut could always be made without difficulty. The model clarified a relationship among rules and valuations. Applying it in practice would require understanding what could be divided and whether the participants could use the procedure as described.

The tutor then distinguished two criteria. Proportionality asked whether a person received at least their own equal-share valuation of the whole. Envy-freeness asked whether they preferred anyone else’s allocation to their own. For two people in this simple setting, the rule connected these ideas closely. With three or more people, receiving at least one third by one’s own measure did not automatically rule out preferring another person’s larger-valued portion.

Other questions remained. A division might need examination for practical cost, strategic behaviour or whether an alternative could make someone better off without making another worse off. Calling an outcome fair did not settle every criterion. The class named which guarantee it was discussing and avoided using one attractive label to certify them all.

Participants could agree to use a rule while still disagree about other goals, so consent to the procedure was recorded separately from its mathematical guarantee.

The exercise made subjectivity explicit without turning reasoning into an arbitrary preference. Given stated valuations and rules, a claim about a criterion could be examined. The productive question was not whether the pieces looked equal to an observer, but which relationship the procedure established for the people involved and which further judgement still needed to be made.

questions.prompt: Why was equal weight not used as a complete fairness criterion?
options: The model assumed nobody valued any part of the cake.
Different people could value the same physical portions differently.
Weight could not be measured in principle.
Market price was guaranteed to match every person’s taste.
questions.explanation: B正确：各部偏好不同，同重不必同满足，故按各自估值。A有不同价值；C非不可称重；D不保证价与味同。

questions.prompt: Why would the cutter not envy the chooser under the stated rule?
options: The chooser had to take the physically smaller part.
The cutter was forbidden to have preferences.
The pieces necessarily had equal market prices.
The cutter had divided the parts to be equal by their own valuation.
questions.explanation: D正确：依假设切者自认两等，不会偏另一份。A选择按偏好不按大小；B有偏好但这两份等；C不要求市场等价。

questions.prompt: What does envy-freeness ask?
options: Whether all participants report the same numerical values.
Whether every portion has identical weight.
Whether a participant prefers someone else’s allocation to their own.
Whether the procedure has no practical cost.
questions.explanation: C正确：定义是不更喜欢他人份；非重量一致、估值共尺或成本为零。B、A、D对应别的属性不在此定义。

questions.prompt: Why does a one-third share for three people not automatically settle envy-freeness?
options: A person can receive an equal-share value and still prefer another allocation.
One third cannot be evaluated by an individual.
Proportionality and envy-freeness are defined as identical for any group size.
All three people must have identical tastes.
questions.explanation: A正确：按自己值达三分一仍可能更偏别人的份，两个标准多人数不必重合。B可自评；C不普同；D无同味假设。

questions.prompt: What is the passage’s main recommendation?
options: Treat every fair label as a guarantee of every desirable property.
State the valuations, procedure and criterion before assessing the claimed guarantee.
Discard formal reasoning whenever tastes differ.
Use physical appearance as the only evidence in every division.
questions.explanation: B正确：结尾把主观估值明示后按规则可核标准，不任意也非一标签全包。A过广；C仍可推理；D外观看等非关键。

units.title: 六级阅读：颜色词的任务作用与地震预警的时间

materials.title: A New Word for a Familiar Colour
materials.text:
A fictional language-and-memory workshop taught participants two new labels for parts of a colour range. After practice, some choices in a memory task changed. The organisers resisted the headline that a new language had changed the participants’ eyes. The task showed a pattern in performance under stated conditions, not a direct measurement of every stage between incoming light and a spoken answer.

The distinction began with the activity itself. Matching two samples visible at the same time differed from recalling one after a delay. A label could help organise attention or provide a remembered category. A changed response in the delayed task did not establish that the same person could now discriminate a smaller physical difference in simultaneous viewing. The report named which task had produced the result.

The labels were also part of the learning situation. Participants had practised sorting and had received instructions about the categories. The resulting behaviour could involve several processes. The team described alternative interpretations rather than assign every observed change to one irreversible transformation in perception. It checked what further comparison would be needed to distinguish a memory aid from a claim about visual sensitivity.

Ordinary colour words had their own contexts of use. A label useful for selecting cloth could organise a practical distinction differently from one used to discuss light or paint. This did not mean any community was unable to notice colours for which it lacked a separate everyday word. A vocabulary described available linguistic tools, not a complete boundary around every experience a speaker could have.

For the public display, the organisers showed how the invented terms had been taught and explained the tasks without requiring visitors to take a colour test. They avoided presenting one participant’s strategy as a rule for all speakers. The examples were useful because they made a relationship between words and an activity visible while leaving the broader mechanism open to investigation.

The organisers retained the exact instructions with the record, because a task described simply as identifying colour could hide different demands on attention, recall and naming.

The account therefore supported neither the view that language could never matter nor the view that a label mechanically determined every act of seeing. It treated words as resources people used in particular tasks. A careful conclusion connected a changed answer to the evidence actually collected and kept attention, memory, naming and sensory discrimination available as distinct questions.

questions.prompt: Why did the organisers reject the claim that participants’ eyes had changed?
options: The task could contain no information about memory.
The participants had learned no labels at all.
They had observed task performance rather than directly established a change in every underlying perceptual process.
Every participant had demonstrated identical visual sensitivity in all conditions.
questions.explanation: C正确：改选择是条件下任务表现，不能直接等同眼睛或全部感知层改变。B有学词；A延迟任务正涉记忆；D未全条件证明同。

questions.prompt: What distinction mattered between simultaneous matching and delayed recall?
options: A memory aid could affect one task without proving finer visual discrimination in the other.
Only delayed recall could involve any attention.
Both were automatically the same operation under different names.
Simultaneous matching required participants to forget every label.
questions.explanation: A正确：词可组织注意分类记忆，延迟改答不证同时辨更小物理差。B非只有延迟注意；C任务不同；D无必须忘词。

questions.prompt: Why describe the training process?
options: It guaranteed that practice had no effect on behaviour.
Instructions and sorting practice were part of the conditions producing the observations.
It proved a permanent change without further comparison.
It removed every alternative interpretation automatically.
questions.explanation: B正确：标签教学、分类练习和指令都构成情境，需后比辨记忆/感度解释。A不保证无影响；C、D过证据。

questions.prompt: What does the passage say about lacking a separate everyday colour word?
options: It necessarily prevents seeing the relevant difference.
It proves that all practical colour distinctions are identical.
It makes speakers unable to learn new tasks.
It does not by itself define a complete limit on the speaker’s possible colour experience.
questions.explanation: D正确：词汇是可用语言工具，不是所有体验边界，不等看不见。A错误；B实践区别可异；C可学新词。

questions.prompt: Which conclusion best reflects the account?
options: Language cannot affect attention or memory in any task.
Labels mechanically determine every visual experience.
Language can matter in a task without its observed effect automatically identifying one universal mechanism of seeing.
One participant’s strategy establishes a rule for every speaker.
questions.explanation: C正确：末段两极都不取，连接具体任务及证据，分注意记忆命名感度。B、A绝对；D不作个人到全体规则。

materials.title: An Alert After the Earthquake Began
materials.text:
An earthquake early-warning system is sometimes described as predicting a quake. A fictional engineering seminar used that description to distinguish two questions. Forecasting an event before it begins differs from detecting an event already under way and sending information before some later effects reach a more distant location.

The early-warning model considered signals from initial ground motion, processing and message transmission. Under suitable conditions, the electronic message could reach a location before a later arriving part of the shaking. That sequence did not mean the source event had waited for the warning. It had begun before the detection that made the message possible.

Distance and delay were crucial. A place close to the source might receive strong motion before the system completed detection and communication. A distant place could have a different available interval. There was no single lead time guaranteed to every recipient. The seminar kept detection time, message issue time and receipt time separate, rather than quote one successful interval as a universal property of the service.

Thresholds involved further decisions. Issuing a message early with limited information could increase unwanted alerts. Waiting for more evidence could reduce some uncertainty while leaving less time. A suitable balance depended on the stated use and the consequences of different errors. Technical improvement could inform that choice without removing it from the design.

Testing therefore examined defined scenarios, network conditions and the outcomes relevant to the intended service. A demonstration of one successful message route was useful evidence, not proof that every future event and recipient would receive the same warning. Records of missed, delayed and unwanted alerts mattered alongside successes.

The number of messages sent also differed from the number of recipients successfully reached. Evaluation kept that denominator visible, along with which devices and connections had been included. A system could improve one stage of transmission while another continued to limit the interval available to a recipient.

The final explanation did not portray early warning as pointless because it could not forecast the exact start of every earthquake. It described the opportunity it sought to use: information can sometimes travel and be processed before a particular effect arrives elsewhere. Its practical claim depended on that timing relationship and the conditions supporting it. Understanding the boundary made the system easier to assess than a broad promise that a computer could tell everyone what would happen before the earthquake existed.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes early warning from the forecasting claim discussed?
options: An early warning always precedes the start of the source event.
It eliminates all processing and communication delay.
It requires every recipient to be located at the source.
It can detect an event already begun and seek to precede later local effects.
questions.explanation: D正确：地震已起后探测，可能赶在远处后续影响前，不是事件未发生预知。A反定义；C不必源近；B延迟关键。

questions.prompt: Why might a nearby location have little or no lead time?
options: The earthquake had to wait until all messages arrived.
Strong motion could arrive before detection and communication were completed.
Nearby receivers never experience ground motion.
The system used the same receipt time for every person by definition.
questions.explanation: B正确：近地强振可先于流程完成，距离与延迟使时窗不同。A因果倒置；C非无振；D不一时刻保证。

questions.prompt: What trade-off is associated with alert thresholds?
options: Earlier decisions can involve less evidence, while waiting can consume available time.
More waiting always creates more lead time.
Earlier messages guarantee there will be no unwanted alert.
Threshold choice removes the consequences of every error.
questions.explanation: A正确：早信息少可能误报，等更证据则时窗少，需按用途权衡。B反；C无保证；D错误后果仍需选择。

questions.prompt: Why record issue and receipt times separately?
options: The message’s wording must change at every station.
Only the source event’s date has a measurable time.
A message being issued is not the same event as it reaching a particular recipient.
Successful examples make every delay irrelevant.
questions.explanation: C正确：检测、发、收不同，个别成功时长不可通化；分记通信阶段。A没说字句站站变；B其他时点可测；D延迟重要。

questions.prompt: How should a successful demonstration be interpreted?
options: As evidence under tested conditions, alongside failures and limits relevant to the intended service.
As proof that all events will produce identical warning intervals.
As proof that the earthquake had not begun when detected.
As a reason to stop collecting records of delayed alerts.
questions.explanation: A正确：限定情境网络及用途，成功与漏延误警并存评估。B外推；C已开始；D记录失败仍必要。
